meta.title: Stationhead, {{spanPhrase}}
meta.description: What happened on Stationhead in {{spanPhrase}}. Artists and fans in the same room, playing the same song, at the same time. Every room can be played back.

og.description: 71,652 streams in fifty five minutes on release day. One in ten people in a room bought the record. {{CountCap}} {{thing}} that happened, all of them replayable.
og.twitterDescription: 71,652 streams in fifty five minutes on release day. One in ten people in a room bought the record.

intro.h1: Stationhead is the home of social listening.
intro.lead: Artists and fans in the same room, playing the same song, at the same time. Every play counts, because every play runs through the listener's own paid account.
body: {{CountCap}} {{thing}} below. All of them happened in {{spanPhrase}}. All of them can be played back right now.

events.herolbl: streams in six days, with nothing being promoted
body: No release, no campaign, no media spend. Fans opened five rooms in six days and streamed eight hundred thousand times. This is the baseline the platform runs at when nobody is doing anything.

events.herolbl: opened on release day, none of them by a label
body: This is what release day looks like here. Three rooms opened on their own, two of them running close to four hours, chat moving between Thai, Indonesian and English while fans posted which room to join so the streams would count.

events.herolbl: streams in fifty five minutes, on release day
body: The group's own account opened the room to mark a release. Fifty five minutes, thirteen songs, and eleven thousand people playing every one of them through their own accounts.
The audience did not need assembling. It was already there, which is the only reason an hour is enough.

events.herolbl: people in the room bought the record

figs.l: of the room were not members

body: Online retail converts in low single digits. This room converted at ten percent, buying while the song played, with no checkout to go and find.
Nobody official ran it. A fan opened the room, and 658 of the people in it were guests who had never signed up for anything.

events.herolbl: chat messages every second, for forty four minutes
body: The occasion was an album turning one year old. Nothing released, nothing announced, nobody paid to post. Ten thousand people came back to a record they already owned and sang it line by line into the chat, in capitals, in time with the track.

events.herolbl: after release, and the room still ran at 321 messages a minute
body: Catalogue does not go quiet here. A three year old album pulled a full room on a Tuesday, and fans put up walls of Brazilian flags and looked after each other while it played.
events.quote: "hi guys i hope yall remember you ARE pretty <3"

events.herolbl: plays in a single day, with the artist hosting
body: Not a drop in. The group hosted their own room four nights running and took the mic every night. This is the ceiling, and the only variable that moved was the artist turning up.

events.herolbl: people came for a label talk, with no band members there
body: The show was billed as label staff talking, with a guest, and said plainly that no members would be there. Five thousand people came anyway and stayed two hours.
The room does not depend on the artist being in it. That is the part worth reading twice.
Her own fan account was hosting. She walked in, spoke for three and a half minutes, then stayed in the chat like everybody else.
The smallest room here and the clearest picture of the whole thing. The audience had already assembled. She just showed up.

pattern.h2: Nobody scheduled almost any of this.
body: A three year old record. Three rooms on release day, none of them opened by a label. A fan account the artist walked into. A room that sold to one person in ten with nobody official running it. Fans opened every one of them.
An artist showing up is what turns one into an event, and the difference here is that the room is already full when they walk in.
pattern.note: Streams are plays of at least thirty seconds, counted inside the room while it was on air, queried from the Stationhead database on {{figureDates}}. The platform totals are as of 10 September 2026. Every play button opens the actual recording. The Paris Paloma figures come from the internal event report for 4 September, and that show has no recording, so it has no play button.

archive.intro: Rooms from earlier weeks. The numbers are as they were reported at the time.

static.h2: It takes a date and an artist handle.
ol: Confirm the channel. If fans built one already, we connect it rather than starting again.
Pick a time that suits the fans, not the office, and tell the regular hosts first. They fill the room before you post anything.
Announce it from the artist account. Date, time, time zone, one link. Nothing else is needed.
Go live from a phone. Connect the streaming account, queue a few songs, then say hello.
On air: read names out, take requests, talk between songs, and say the room stays open when you go.
static.note: One week is comfortable. Two days is possible.

static.when: What you can put in the room
static.h2: Four things, all of them quick.
ul: Digital purchase. The single or album, bought in the room while it plays. About a week.
Shopify shop. Your existing store, opened inside the room. About a week.
Voice note. Thirty seconds recorded on a phone, for when a live date will not work. Two days.
Fan Channel. The permanent room fans join once and keep between releases. A few days.
static.note: To start we need the artist handle, a date, and anything you want to sell.
